item.title: Amazon QuickSight Layer Maps Add Point and LineString Geometry Support
item.description:
Amazon QuickSight Layer Maps Add Point and LineString Geometry Support

Amazon QuickSight now lets layer maps display individual locations and routes by supporting Point and LineString geometry types from GeoJSON files.

🔍 Overview

  • Layer maps can plot points and routes, such as store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport.
  • Supports multiple map types: point maps, filled maps, and layer maps.
  • Geospatial maps help businesses spot location‑tied patterns, like regional performance or customer concentration.

🧩 How it works

  • A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a QuickSight dataset; a shared key joins the two.
  • GeoJSON requirements: saved with a .geojson extension, maximum file size 100 MB, geometry types include Point, LineString, and Polygon.
  • Configuration settings:
    1. Geometry type to visualize – selects which geometry (Points, Lines, or Polygons) from the GeoJSON file is rendered. Only one type appears at a time.
    2. Shape‑file key ↔ dataset key – matches a key field in the GeoJSON properties to a key field in the dataset. Field names can differ, but values must match.
  • Example workflow for routes:
    • GeoJSON holds one LineString feature per route, keyed by route_id.
    • QuickSight dataset has one row per route, also keyed by route_id.
    • Set Geometry type to Lines; the visual draws each path from the ordered coordinates in the GeoJSON file.
  • Example workflow for points:
    • GeoJSON holds one Point feature per store or facility, keyed by a store ID.
    • Dataset has one row per store.
    • Set Geometry type to Points.

⚙️ Key details

  • New geometry support: Point (marks specific locations) and LineString (traces routes such as deliveries, flights, shipping lanes, pipelines).
  • Layer map visual behavior:
    • Draws paths from GeoJSON coordinates rather than generating them from data at load time.
    • Join key in GeoJSON ties each LineString to the dataset row that provides tooltip and color information.
  • File format: GeoJSON is a JSON‑based format describing geographic features; each feature’s geometry has a type (Point, LineString, Polygon) and coordinates.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables businesses to visualize not just regions (handled by polygons) but also the exact locations of assets and the routes connecting them.
  • Supports use cases such as:
    • Mapping flights leaving an airport.
    • Visualizing delivery paths for logistics.
    • Showing shipping lanes or pipeline segments.
  • By joining geographic shapes to dataset metrics, teams can overlay performance data on routes or locations for deeper insight.

#AmazonQuickSight #GeospatialBI #LayerMaps #GeoJSON #DataVisualization

Source: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps | Amazon Web Services

item.title: OlmoEarth v1.3 releases global 10‑m satellite embeddings and explorer
item.description:
OlmoEarth v1.3 releases global 10‑m satellite embeddings and explorer

Today the team released OlmoEarth v1.3, a state‑of‑the‑art satellite embedding model that generates a 128‑dimensional vector for every 10‑meter pixel on Earth and ships with pre‑computed global embeddings and a browser‑based explorer.

🚀 Release

  • OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a full year of Sentinel‑1 radar and Sentinel‑2/Landsat multispectral time series.
  • It outputs a 128‑dimensional vector per pixel; the first 64 dimensions can be used independently.
  • Pre‑computed annual embeddings are provided for the entire planet at 10 m resolution in both 64‑ and 128‑dimensional forms.
  • The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer lets anyone pan, flip years, and compare vectors without signing in or advanced technical knowledge.

🧩 How it works

  • A vision transformer ingests the satellite data.
  • An Attention Pooler aggregates the data into one vector per land patch.
  • A linear layer reduces the pooled representation to 128 numbers.

📊 Evaluation & Performance

Variant Dimensions Leads on evals (out of 27)
OlmoEarth v1.3 (full) 128 20
OlmoEarth v1.3 (half) 64 18
  • The 128‑dimensional embeddings scored highest on 20 of 27 evaluations and ranked highest overall against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2.
  • The 64‑dimensional version still led on 18 of 27 evaluations.
  • A new PLANTEUR crop‑type benchmark for tropical farming was introduced; OlmoEarth embeddings generalized best to unseen locations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Training cost: roughly $2,720 of rented H100 GPU time for the final run.
  • Compared to v1.2, training time dropped to 53% and carbon emissions to 50%; compared to v1, time dropped to 18% and emissions to 22%.
  • Model weights, pre‑training data, and code are fully open on Source Cooperative.

📈 Availability & Tools

  • The pre‑computed embeddings are shared publicly; users can train a small classifier locally for tasks such as:
    • Smallholder‑crop classification in Kenya
    • Brick‑kiln detection west of Dhaka
    • Fire‑damage assessment in Indonesia
    • Gold‑mining monitoring in the Peruvian Amazon
  • The Embeddings Explorer renders the embeddings as a false‑color map, allows year‑to‑year comparison, and lets users click a location to find similar places or drop labeled points to train a classifier on the fly.

💡 Why it matters

  • Global embeddings turn heavyweight satellite analysis into lightweight, locally‑run models.
  • In Peru’s Madre de Dios region, the embeddings highlighted illegal gold‑mining expansion from 2017‑2020 and subsequent shifts through 2025, matching on‑the‑ground reports from MAAP and the Associated Press.
  • By lowering compute and expertise barriers, the release aims to democratize high‑resolution Earth observation for research, NGOs, and industry.

#Satellites #Embeddings #OpenSource #GeospatialAI

Source: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
